title: The sandbox removes the global names but leaves a live context binding: `this` still walks back to the host runtime
index_line: T-0021 · CODE_EXEC · expression sandbox blocks `require`, leaves `this`→`process`→module system · node/any-embedded-JS · corroborated
invariant_violated: An expression evaluator is assumed safe because it removes or shadows the dangerous global names (`require`, `process`, `global`). But the evaluated function is still *called with a receiver*, and the receiver's prototype chain reaches the same runtime. Denying names does not deny reachability.

mechanism.does: the attacker (or a chained read primitive) gets the right to author an expression in a field the server evaluates
the evaluator hides the host globals from the expression's scope and runs it inside a function-like wrapper
the wrapper is invoked with a receiver, so `this` resolves to a context object rather than to undefined
walking the receiver's prototype/constructor chain reaches the host `process` object — a name that was never in scope
`process.mainModule` (or the module cache) exposes the full module loader, so `require('child_process')` becomes available after all
the child process runs with the privileges of the application process, which is the whole prize

source.http.body.value: the workflow/node/step field that carries a `{{ }}` expression — the attacker does not send code, they send a field value that will be compiled

sink.eval.value: the expression compile+run call (new Function, vm.runInContext, lodash template, a rules/expressions DSL)

gadget.engine-escape.value: `this` → `process` → `mainModule.require` (or `constructor.constructor`), the path from a sandboxed expression to the module system

guard.sandbox.value: the denylist/shadow of global names — it is defeated because it enumerates names rather than severing the receiver

preconditions.expr: server-side expression evaluation exists and is reachable by the attacker's privilege level
the attacker can author a value that is evaluated (workflow editor, rules engine, template field, formula)
the sandbox hides global *names* — confirm the evaluated function still receives a receiver (a `this` inside it is not undefined)

check.spec: send an expression that returns typeof this and Object.getPrototypeOf(this); a non-undefined receiver with a reachable constructor chain is the precondition

preconditions.expr: the process runs with more privilege than the workflow author should have (in the stock container, root)

success: the expression returns the output of an OS command (`uid=0(root)` style) rather than a value the app computed
the escape uses no application feature — only runtime internals that should not have been reachable from the expression
a child process appears under the application's process, spawning a shell or a downloader
failure_like: `this` is undefined in the evaluated scope, or the receiver is a frozen null-prototype object
the evaluator ships a real isolate/process boundary (separate worker with a message-only channel) rather than a name denylist
false_positive: an expression that merely *mentions* `process` in a string and is never evaluated (stored, logged, or rendered as text)
client-side evaluation only — browser `eval` on the attacker's own page is not this
a crash or timeout from an infinite loop — availability, not code execution

hazards: the escape shape is runtime-specific and version-specific — `mainModule` is deprecated-but-present in some builds; enumerate a few receiver paths before concluding safe
the precondition is usually the hard part: this needs authoring rights, which is why it is so often chained with an unauthenticated read that forges a session
running the process as non-root does not fix the bug, it lowers the blast radius — say so, do not confuse the two
non_transfers: engines that evaluate in a separate process or WASM isolate with no shared objects
engines with a real AST allow-list (no member access on arbitrary receivers) rather than a name denylist
pure data-binding templates that never evaluate operators/functions
